criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community urban sanitation service access and distributive inequalities across eight socio-technical sanitation regimes in Nairobi (sewered household toilets, sewered shared toilets, emptied onsite tanks, container-based shared toilets, unemptied/unsafely managed household and shared toilets, public toilets, and coping/open defecation).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — conducts a deductive NVivo review of national and county constitutional, statutory, regulatory, planning, and investment frameworks governing Nairobi's sanitation sector and climate adaptation. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Borderline yes — although the overarching framing centres on climate adaptation mainstreaming and master-plan sewerage capital investment ('fantasy planning' vs 'business-as-usual'), the empirical policy/legal analysis directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access, including utility regulatory structure and statutory service mandates (Water Act, CIDP, NIUPLAN, and NCWSC's sewerage-only mandate excluding non-sewered regimes from public provision; WASREB excluding its Pro-poor Service Assessment from core utility performance ranking metrics), tariff/levy and cost-recovery rules (WASREB's unimplemented sanitation levy guidelines, cost-recovery/commercialisation incentives deterring low-income and non-sewered service, and lack of public subsidy contracts for container-based sanitation), and regulatory accommodation in urban planning (suspension of conventional planning regulations in the Mukuru Special Planning Area).
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining geospatial mapping and WorldPop 100x100m gridded population analysis (2022 baseline and 2030 ArcGIS time-series spatial forecast) with deductive qualitative content coding (NVivo) of primary national and county laws, regulatory guidelines, strategic plans, and donor/government budgets, validated with sector stakeholders.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports current (2022) and projected (2030) spatial and population access/exclusion across sanitation service regimes in Nairobi (4.56M residents in 2022, with <1/3 in adequate household regimes, ~40% in unsafe/inadequate regimes, and stagnant 50% sewer coverage; 6.13M projected in 2030 with rising numbers in inadequate/coping regimes), plus climate-hazard disruption to toilet and sewer access.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (Nairobi City County residents across spatial sub-areas/100m grid cells and eight sanitation regimes; national and county legal/planning instruments), exposure (sewer-centric statutory, regulatory, cost-recovery, and planning/investment frameworks and climate adaptation policies), outcome (population and spatial distribution across sanitation access regimes in 2022 and 2030), and study design (mixed-methods geospatial + deductive qualitative document analysis case study) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining geospatial and gridded population raster analysis (2022 baseline mapping and 2030 time-series spatial forecasting) with deductive qualitative policy/legal document content analysis (NVivo) and stakeholder validation.
population_and_sample: Urban population of Nairobi City County, Kenya (approx. 4,560,000 residents in 2022 baseline and 6,130,000 projected in 2030 across 100x100m WorldPop grid cells and residential land-use sub-areas), alongside reviewed national and county sanitation and climate legal, regulatory, planning, and investment documents.
exposure: National and county sanitation and climate-adaptation legal, regulatory, planning, and public-finance frameworks in Nairobi (including statutory/utility sewerage-only mandates under the Water Act, CIDP, NIUPLAN, and NCWSC Strategic Plan excluding non-sewered sanitation; WASREB pro-poor regulatory reporting and unimplemented sanitation levy guidelines; cost-recovery/commercialisation orientation; and Mukuru Special Planning Area planning-rule accommodation).
outcome: Spatial and population distribution of household and community access to eight sanitation service regimes across Nairobi in 2022 and projected to 2030 (including sewered household/shared connections, emptied tanks, container-based sanitation, unsafely managed onsite toilets, public toilets, and coping/lack of toilet access, alongside citywide sewer coverage and climate-related loss of access).
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study maps sanitation service access and exclusion across Nairobi (2022 baseline and 2030 projection) and uses deductive NVivo coding to evaluate national and county legal, regulatory, planning, and investment frameworks. While its overarching framing focuses on climate adaptation planning and infrastructure investment ('fantasy planning' vs 'business-as-usual' sewerage expansion), its qualitative socio-legal and policy analysis directly examines rule-type mechanisms under Criterion 2—including statutory and utility mandates excluding non-sewered sanitation regimes from public provision, WASREB regulatory ranking and sanitation levy rules, cost-recovery/commercialisation barriers to serving low-income unsewered areas, and planning-rule accommodation in the Mukuru Special Planning Area—and links this sewer-centric governance trajectory to citywide sanitation access and exclusion outcomes. Per protocol safeguards, mechanism-relevant qualitative/mixed-methods socio-legal studies are included even without a household-level econometric effect estimate; confidence is set to medium given the borderline macro-planning framing.
